slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: “Ellen **and** Mary study botany.” — *Ellen* and *Mary* are both used as the subject:  something is affirmed of each.  *and* connects them.
“Ellen **or** Mary studies botany.” — at least one of them is represented as studying.  *or* connects them.
“Ellen will study botany, **if** Mary studies algebra.” — two clauses;  *if* connects them.
Words used merely to join words or groups of words are called *Conjunctions*.

slides.text: A Conjunction is a word used to connect words, phrases, clauses, and members.
examples: He looked under the bed **and** behind the door.  (phrases)
Eli and Silas will improve, **if** they study.  (clauses)
Wheat grows in the field, **and** men reap it.  (members — the sentences joined in a compound sentence)

rows.sentence: Eli and Silas will improve, if they study.
rows.note: *if* connects clauses.  *if they study* is an adverbial element:  it hangs from *will improve* inside one diagram.

rows.sentence: Wheat grows in the field, and men reap it.
rows.note: *and* connects members.  Each member is diagrammed as a sentence by itself;  neither is an element of the other.

slides.heading: Conjunction or Preposition?
bullets: Conjunctions merely connect;  unlike prepositions, they do not express relations.
“He is a man **of** wealth.” — *of* shows the relation of its object, *wealth*, to *man*.
“Ellen **and** Mary study botany.” — *and* only joins;  *Mary* is not its object.
Some words serve as both:  “Wait **until** noon” (preposition — object *noon*);  “Wait **until** I come” (conjunction — joins clauses).

slides.heading: Practice — Point Out the Conjunctions (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Name each conjunction and what it connects.  Model — “Eli and Silas will improve, if they study.” — and:  Eli · Silas;  if:  the clauses Eli and Silas will improve · they study.
items: We moved along silently and cautiously.
I consent to the constitution, because I expect no better.
He heaped up great riches, but passed his time miserably.
answers: because:  the clauses I consent to the constitution · I expect no better
but:  the predicates heaped up great riches · passed his time miserably

slides.heading: Practice — Point Out the Conjunctions (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Name each conjunction and what it connects.  Model — “Eli and Silas will improve, if they study.” — and:  Eli · Silas;  if:  the clauses Eli and Silas will improve · they study.
items: He is both learned and wise.
I shall not go, if it rain.  (*if it rain* = *if it should rain*)
Cold and hunger awake not her care.  (*awake not* = *do not awaken*)
answers: if:  the clauses I shall not go · it rain

slides.heading: Practice — Point Out the Conjunctions (Set 3)
slides.instruction: Name each conjunction and what it connects.  Model — “Eli and Silas will improve, if they study.” — and:  Eli · Silas;  if:  the clauses Eli and Silas will improve · they study.
items: They submit, since they can not conquer.
He has many faults, still he is very popular.
Emma or Susan will remain at home.
answers: since:  the clauses They submit · they can not conquer
still:  the members He has many faults · he is very popular

slides.heading: Practice — Conjunction or Preposition?
slides.instruction: Tell whether the marked word is a conjunction or a preposition.  If a preposition, name its object.
items: He is poor, **but** honest.
All **but** one escaped.
**Since** you ask, I will tell you.
I have not seen him **since** Monday.
We rested **after** dinner.
He rose **before** daybreak.
We rested **after** we had dined.
He rose **before** the sun was up.

slides.heading: Oral Lesson — Compound Elements
bullets: “James and Samuel are kind, honest, and faithful.”
*James* and *Samuel* are the parts of a *Compound Subject*.
*kind*, *honest*, and *faithful* are the parts of a *Compound Predicate*.

slides.text: A Compound Element consists of two or more similar parts of the same proposition connected by conjunctions.
examples: We **run, jump, and talk** at recess.  (predicate)
My father owns **a farm and a factory**.  (objective element)
Tray is a **large, black, and cross** dog.  (adjective element;  *cross* = surly)

slides.heading: Remarks on Compound Elements
bullets: Rem. 1. — The conjunctions may be expressed or understood:  in “We run, jump, and talk,” an *and* is understood between *run* and *jump*.  Any element of a proposition may be compound.
*Similar* parts are of the same kind:  subjects with subjects, predicates with predicates, modifiers with modifiers.
A compound element is still one proposition:  in “James and Samuel are kind,” one copula, *are*, affirms *kind* of the subject *James and Samuel* — though it says what two propositions would.

slides.heading: Compound Elements & Truth
bullets: “James and Samuel are kind” = *James is kind* and *Samuel is kind*:  true if both are true;  false if either is false.
“Ellen or Mary studies botany”:  true if at least one studies;  false only if neither does.
“**Either** Ellen **or** Mary studies botany”:  true if exactly one studies;  false if neither does, or both do.
Not every *and* divides so:  “Rome and Carthage were rivals” does not mean “Rome was rivals.”  The predicate is affirmed of the parts taken together.

rows.note: Declarative. *William and Henry* is the compound subject;  *study*, the predicate.  *study* is modified by *algebra*, an objective element.

rows.sentence: James and Samuel are kind, honest, and faithful.
rows.note: Declarative. *James and Samuel* is the compound subject;  *kind, honest, and faithful*, the compound predicate;  *are*, the copula.

rows.sentence: Mr. Edson buys and sells butter and eggs.
rows.note: Declarative. *Mr. Edson* is the subject;  *buys and sells*, the compound predicate, which is modified by *butter and eggs*, a compound objective element.

rows.sentence: The two boys moved along silently and cautiously.
rows.note: Declarative. *boys* is the subject;  *moved*, the predicate.  *boys* is modified by *the* and *two*, adjective elements;  *moved*, by *along*, an adverbial element, and by *silently and cautiously*, a compound adverbial element.

rows.sentence: Exercise and temperance strengthen the constitution.
rows.note: *Exercise and temperance*, the compound subject;  *strengthen*, the predicate;  *constitution*, an objective element.

rows.sentence: Your levity and heedlessness will prevent all improvement.
rows.note: *levity and heedlessness*, the compound subject, modified by *Your*;  *will prevent*, the predicate;  *improvement*, an objective element.

rows.sentence: Duty and interest forbid vicious and wicked indulgences.
rows.note: *Duty and interest*, the compound subject;  *vicious and wicked*, a compound adjective element modifying *indulgences*.

rows.sentence: Mr. Mann owns and cultivates a large and valuable farm.
rows.note: *owns and cultivates*, the compound predicate;  *large and valuable*, a compound adjective element modifying *farm*.

rows.sentence: Forty pupils study arithmetic, grammar, and geography.
rows.note: *pupils*, the subject;  *study*, the predicate;  *arithmetic, grammar, and geography*, a compound objective element.

rows.sentence: The wearied soldiers fought bravely and successfully.
rows.note: *soldiers*, the subject;  *fought*, the predicate, modified by *bravely and successfully*, a compound adverbial element.

slides.heading: Directions for Writing
bullets: More than two parts:  I. Place a comma after each part except the last.  II. Use the conjunction between the last two parts only. — “kind, honest, and faithful”
Two parts:  I. Connect them by a conjunction — “Ellen and Lucy.”  II. Or, omit the conjunction and use a comma in its stead — “a tall, slender tree.”
Rem. 2. — To make the parts emphatic, the conjunction and the comma may both be used between any two of them:  “kind, and honest, and faithful.”

slides.heading: Recall — Commas with Adjectives
bullets: Adjectives that form a compound element take commas — the comma stands in for an understood *and*:  a cold, dreary, endless night.
Test — coordinate adjectives can take *and* between them or be reversed:  “a cold and dreary night”;  “a dreary, cold night.”
If you can’t insert *and* or reverse them, they aren’t coordinate but cumulative — so no commas:  “a little old wooden chair” (not “a wooden old little chair”).
Never put a comma between the last adjective and its noun:  a kind, gentle man  (no comma after gentle).

slides.heading: Practice — Comma or No Comma?
slides.instruction: Add a comma between coordinate adjectives (those you could join with *and*); use none between cumulative adjectives. Write each phrase correctly.
items: a cold dreary night
a big black dog
a brave honest man
an old stone bridge
a dark stormy sky
a tall wooden fence
a kind gentle teacher
a red silk dress

slides.heading: Practice — Punctuate the Compound Elements
slides.instruction: Write each compound element correctly, following the Directions for Writing.
items: The farmer plows sows and reaps.
She bought apples pears and plums.
The horse was old lame and blind.
The wind blew fiercely steadily and coldly.
It was a long dull day.
They lived in a little brick house.
Mary and Jane sing in the choir.
Exercise temperance and rest strengthen the constitution.
answers: long, dull  or  long and dull

rows.sentence: A tall, slender, and graceful tree shaded the house.
rows.note: Coordinate:  *tall, slender, and graceful* is a compound adjective element — one dashed line joins all three parts.

rows.sentence: A little old stone house stood there.
rows.note: Cumulative:  *A*, *little*, *old*, and *stone* are separate adjective elements, each on its own line under *house*.  No *and* fits between them, so no commas.

slides.heading: The Order of Cumulative Adjectives
bullets: Cumulative adjectives keep a set order — *little old stone*, not *stone old little*:  OSASCOMP.
Opinion · Size · Age · Shape · Color · Origin · Material · Purpose — then the noun.
“A **lovely little old round red French wooden writing** desk stood in the corner.” — each adjective in its slot.
Reorder them and it sounds foreign:  “A **wooden red little lovely** desk stood in the corner.”
A strong tendency, not a strict rule.

answers: A word used to connect words, phrases, clauses, and members.
A conjunction merely connects;  a preposition expresses a relation and has an object.
Two or more similar parts of the same proposition connected by conjunctions.
Yes — they may be expressed or understood.
A comma after each part except the last;  the conjunction between the last two parts only.
